query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Lightweight high-entropy alloys that are compositionally engineered to form a homogeneous single‐phase microstructure (via high configurational entropy) can simultaneously achieve low density, high mechanical strength, superior corrosion resistance, and excellent high‐temperature oxidation resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous, protective oxide layer (e.g., Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3). In contrast, alloys that develop even minor elemental segregations (such as Cu-rich phases) will exhibit impaired passivation and reduced mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: A lightweight high-entropy alloy base system incorporating low-density elements (e.g., Al, Ti, V) with additional elements (e.g., Cr, V, and trace Cu) that can be tuned to either yield a homogeneous single-phase structure or induce phase segregation.
generation.intervention: Conduct a controlled compositional adjustment study in which the alloy is processed in two ways: one set is optimized for homogeneous mixing (minimizing segregation) and the other is intentionally doped (e.g., with increased Cu content) to promote local segregation.
generation.conditions: Evaluate the alloys under corrosive conditions (e.g., immersion in 0.6 M NaCl solution) and high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., exposure to air at ~900 °C) while performing mechanical tests (tensile/compression) at ambient conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform, single-phase matrix with nanoscale chemical fluctuations that permits the in-situ formation of a continuous, dense oxide film (predominantly Al2O3/Cr2O3) during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy stabilizes the single-phase microstructure and induces pronounced lattice distortion, which enhances solid-solution strengthening. Simultaneously, the nanostructural uniformity facilitates rapid, uniform passivation through the formation of a protective oxide layer. In alloys with induced elemental segregation, discontinuities in the oxide film lead to localized galvanic cells, adversely affecting corrosion resistance and mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys processed for homogeneity will exhibit higher yield strength, lower corrosion current densities, slower oxidation kinetics (lower mass gain), and better overall performance compared to alloys engineered with minor segregation (e.g., via excess Cu addition).
generation.baseline: A comparable lightweight HEA with a tendency for phase segregation (for instance, higher Cu content causing Cu-rich areas) that shows inferior mechanical strength, higher corrosion current densities, and faster oxidation rates.
generation.boundary: The hypothesized performance benefits will no longer hold if compositional adjustments lead to a critical level of phase separation where even the homogeneous matrix is disrupted, or if processing conditions fail to achieve sufficient atomic mixing.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between specific elemental concentrations, the degree of lattice distortion, and the resulting oxide film integrity is not yet fully determined, and there remains uncertainty regarding the optimal thresholds for preventing segregation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two series of lightweight high-entropy alloy samples with identical base compositions. Process one series using optimized rapid solidification or high-energy milling to secure a homogeneous single-phase microstructure. Process the second series with modified casting conditions and deliberate addition of a segregation-prone element (e.g., increased Cu content) to induce elemental clustering. Subject both series to standardized tensile testing, potentiodynamic corrosion measurements in 0.6 M NaCl, and high-temperature oxidation testing at 900 °C.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ductility at ambient temperature
Electrochemical corrosion current density and pitting potential
Oxidation kinetics measured as mass gain over time at 900 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy series with induced segregation (higher Cu content) exhibits mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance metrics that are statistically indistinguishable from the homogeneous alloy series, then the hypothesis that a homogeneous single-phase microstructure and consequent protective oxide formation underlie the multifunctional performance is falsified.

A Lightweight AlCrTiV0.5Cux High-Entropy Alloy with Excellent Corrosion Resistance

Abstract: Lightweight high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of low-density, high strength-to-weight ratio metallic structural material. Understanding their corrosion behavior is crucial for designing microstructures for their practical applications. This work investigates the electrochemical corrosion behavior of lightweight HEAs AlCrTiV0.5Cux (x = 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0) in a 0.6 M NaCl solution. These HEAs were produced by vacuum arc melting. In contrast to 304L stainless steel, all of the alloys exhibited lower current density levels caused by self-corrosion, with AlCrTiV0.5 demonstrating the highest corrosion resistance (0.131 μA/cm2). Corrosion resistance decreased along with the content of copper because copper segregation accelerated local corrosion throughout the alloy.

Effects of Cold Rolling or Precipitation Hardening Treatment on the Microstructure, Mechanical Properties, and Corrosion Resistance of Ti-Rich Metastable Medium-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractTitanium-rich metastable medium-entropy alloys, designed for low elastic moduli, sacrifice strength. However, enhancing their mechanical strength is crucial for bio-implant applications. This study aims to enhance the mechanical properties and corrosion resistance of a metastable Ti80–Nb10–Mo5–Sn5 medium-entropy alloy using various treatments, including cold rolling (at 50% and 75% reduction) and precipitation hardening (at room temperature, 150 °C, 350 °C, 550 °C, and 750 °C). The results showed that the alloy underwent a stress-induced martensitic transformation during the rolling process. Notably, the α phase was precipitated in the β grain boundaries after 30 days of precipitation hardening at room temperature. Remarkable Enhanced Mechanical Properties of TiAlCrNbV Medium-Entropy Alloy with Zr Additions

Abstract: Most medium entropy alloys (MEAs) exhibit excellent mechanical properties, but their applications are limited because of their high density. This study explores a series of lightweight nonequiatomic Ti65(AlCrNbV)35-xZrx (x = 3, 5, 7, and 10) MEAs with a low density, high strength, and high ductility. To achieve solid solution strengthening, Zr with a large atomic radius was used. In addition, various thermomechanical treatment parameters were adopted to further improve the MEAs’ mechanical properties. The density of the MEAs was revealed to be approximately 5 g/cm3, indicating that they were lightweight. Through an X-ray diffraction analysis, the MEAs were revealed to have a single body-centered cubic structure not only in the as-cast state but also after thermomechanical treatment. A Lightweight AlTiVNb High-Entropy Alloy Film with High Strength-Ductility Synergy and Corrosion Resistance

Abstract: The simultaneous improvement of mechanical and corrosion resistance is of great significance for engineering applications. In this work, a novel lightweight amorphous structure AlTiVNb high-entropy alloy (HEA) film was fabricated by magnetron sputtering. The compression test of the AlTiVNb HEA film nanopillar exhibits a high compressive strength of up to 3.6 GPa and deformability approaching 58%. The high strength is affected by the disordered state, the nanostructure, and the lattice distortion effect, while the high ductility comes from the ductile shear band and the island structure. In addition, the AlTiVNb HEA film shows a current density of 4.90 × 10−8 A/cm2 and a potential of −0.234 V in the 3.5% NaCl solution, comparable to that of the 316L stainless steel. The chemical disorder state, cocktail effect, and homogeneous amorphous structure contribute to excellent corrosion resistance. This finding offers new insights into high-performance HEA films with robust mechanical and anticorrosion performances for microelectronic devices and mechanical metamaterials.
